items.question: Is contrarianism easier to practice than most people think?
items.challenge_reason: Many would argue that genuine contrarianism requires deep conviction and rigorous thinking, making it harder than simply saying 'no' to consensus.

cast.text:
Contrarianism is acc easier than most people think: you just need to say "no" when everyone else is saying "yes". A person can disagree with others for more than conviction or principles--we have dumb contrarian opinions for a reason. 

Moreover, the incentives are twisted: there's a hidden bias that makes us automatically believe a contrarian take must be true because it's different from everything else we hear. Flat earthers and conspiracy theorists would get less attention and credibility if this bias was absent. 

But reverse stupidity isn't intelligence (https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/qNZM3EGoE5ZeMdCRt/reversed-stupidity-is-not-intelligence). If everyone says meat is good and you say "meat is bad", your hypothesis might be incorrect. Eeryone could be right on the issue, while you're wrong.

If anything, knowing this will help reduce the number of bad contrarian takes that we see in the world today imo. Your "unpopular opinion" may be unpopular because people have enough sense to know it's wrong. :)

members.reason: Many would argue that genuine contrarianism requires deep conviction and rigorous thinking, making it harder than simply saying 'no' to consensus.

cast.text:
Great point 🫡 

There are people who are contrarians by default - we all met this one rebellious kid in high school or college. 

Funnily, being "that kid" on social media is a pretty powerful tactic since contrarian takes naturally stand out which means they generate attention.

members.reason: The reply affirms the parent's core claim that contrarianism is easy by citing the example of default contrarians and emphasizing how contrarian takes naturally stand out and generate attention—reinforcing the parent's argument that one can easily practice contrarianism by simply opposing consensus.

cast.text:
Yudkowsky has a good thesis on why/how to differentiate "rebellion because it makes me look cool" from "rebellion because I have solid reasons to disagree with everyone else on the topic": https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/CEGnJBHmkcwPTysb7/lonely-dissent. Oh, and the "contrarian takes generate attention" point is the twisted incentives I'm talking about.

I try to avoid falling into the trap myself, even if it's difficult. Always helps to try and steelman the opposing argument before sharing opinions publicly.

members.reason: The reply endorses and elaborates on the parent's point about contrarian takes generating attention (linking it to the root's 'twisted incentives'), and adds supporting detail via Yudkowsky's framework for distinguishing genuine dissent from performative rebellion. The author is reinforcing their original stance with additional evidence.

items.question: Is Aptos's encrypted mempool a meaningful advance in MEV protection?
items.challenge_reason: Skeptics argue encrypted mempools don't solve MEV in practice if validators can still observe or collude post-reveal, and that adoption will be too low to matter.

cast.text:
Aptos shipped an encrypted mempool on mainnet that hides transaction payloads until block finalization, using the same validator set already trusted for consensus. It is opt-in per transaction, so everyday users can ignore it while institutions and agents gain protection against front-running without introducing new trust assumptions. The added gas cost and modest latency are explicit. Real impact will show up in whether large flows and automated systems actually choose the option when markets are moving, rather than in the cryptography itself.

Source: https://aptosnetwork.com/currents/encrypted-mempool-mainnet

members.reason: Skeptics argue encrypted mempools don't solve MEV in practice if validators can still observe or collude post-reveal, and that adoption will be too low to matter.
